samples.text:
Many people like to learn about the history of their town or city. This essay will explain why people enjoy this and how local history can be more interesting for young generation.

There are some reasons why people are interested in local history. Firstly, it helps them to understand their identity. When people know how their town was built and what happened there in the past, they feel more proud and connected to their home. Secondly, local history is easier to imagine than world history because people can see the old buildings, bridges or monuments every day. For example, if there is an old castle in the city, people are curious to know who lived there. Also, some people learn about local history because their own family lived in the area for many years and they want to know about their grandparents life.

However, many young people think history is boring because they only read books and remember dates at school. There are some ways to change this. First, schools can organise trips to museums and historical places, so students can see things with their own eyes. Second, technology can be used, for example apps or videos which shows how the town looked hundred years ago. Young people love technology, so this will attract them. Another idea is to invite old people from the community to school to tell stories about the past, which is more interesting than a textbook.

In conclusion, people enjoy local history because it gives them identity and it is easy to connect with. To make it interesting for young people, schools should use trips, technology and stories from older people instead of only books.
samples.why: Both questions answered with relevant, familiar ideas · limited development and some repetition · mechanical sequencing (Firstly, Second) · adequate vocabulary with some wrong choices (remember dates) · errors in articles, possessives and agreement.

samples.text:
Local history attracts a surprising amount of interest, with many people visiting museums, joining heritage walks or reading about the origins of their town. This essay will discuss the reasons for this interest and suggest ways to make the subject more engaging for younger generations.

One important reason is that local history provides a sense of identity and belonging. Knowing how a community developed, for example why a market town grew up beside a particular river or how local industries shaped the lives of previous residents, helps people feel rooted in the place where they live. Local history is also more tangible than national or global events. People pass historic buildings, statues and street names every day, and learning the stories behind them makes familiar surroundings more meaningful. In addition, many people have a personal connection to the past through their own families, and researching local records can reveal how their ancestors lived and worked.

Young people, however, often regard history as a dry subject, so it needs to be presented in more active ways. One effective approach is to take learning out of the classroom. Guided visits to historic sites, or projects in which students investigate the history of their own street, allow them to discover information for themselves rather than memorise facts. Technology can also help. Interactive apps could show teenagers how a square looked centuries ago, while local museums could use social media to share short and entertaining stories. Finally, involving older residents is valuable, as hearing first-hand accounts of how the town has changed make the past feel real and personal.

In conclusion, people enjoy local history because it strengthens their identity and connects them with familiar places and their own families. For young people, hands-on projects, digital tools and contact with older generations can transform it into a lively and relevant subject.
samples.why: Both parts answered clearly with extended, well-illustrated ideas · clear topic for each paragraph · good range of vocabulary (tangible, rooted, first-hand accounts) · mostly accurate structures with one agreement slip.

samples.text:
For many people, the history of their own town or region holds an appeal that grand narratives of empires and wars cannot match. This enthusiasm stems largely from the personal and tangible nature of local history, and although young people are often less engaged, there are effective ways of bringing the subject to life for them.

The most fundamental reason is that local history helps people understand who they are. Learning why a village grew up around a particular crossroads, or how a factory once sustained an entire neighbourhood, gives residents a sense of continuity that can be especially valuable in a rapidly changing world. Local history is also immediate in a way that national history rarely is. The evidence is visible in everyday surroundings, from the architecture of the high street to the names of lanes and pubs, so each discovery transforms a familiar route into something richer. Finally, it often intersects with family history; parish records or old photographs may reveal where one's great-grandparents worked or worshipped, creating a direct emotional link with the past.

Engaging young people requires moving away from passive learning. Rather than being presented with dates and summaries, students could act as historians themselves, interviewing elderly residents, examining old maps or investigating the history of their own school. Such projects give them ownership of their findings and reveal that history is made up of real people's lives. Digital technology offers further possibilities: augmented reality apps can overlay historical images onto present-day streets, and short video formats allow students to share what they have uncovered in a style that appeals to their peers. Local museums, too, can attract younger audiences with interactive exhibitions rather than static displays.

In conclusion, local history resonates with people because it strengthens identity, gives meaning to familiar places and connects them with their ancestors. By encouraging active investigation and embracing digital media, schools and museums can make it equally compelling for the young.
samples.why: Both questions fully answered with well-developed, specific ideas · logical sequencing and seamless cohesion · wide, precise vocabulary (continuity, intersects, ownership of their findings) · wide range of error-free structures.
